title: Tensions Escalate: Pakistan Warns of Potential Conflict with India | Politics
content: Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif warned on October 8, 2025, that the chances of war with India are real, asserting that Pakistan is better positioned for any future conflict and would achieve greater success in such a scenario. Speaking to Samaa TV, Asif emphasized that while Pakistan does not seek escalation, the threat of conflict cannot be ignored. He highlighted increased national unity and a notable shift in international alliances, stating that Pakistan now enjoys greater international support compared to six months prior. His remarks follow escalating tensions after India's Operation Sindoor, launched in response to a terror attack in April 2025, which triggered a temporary ceasefire. The exchange of threats between Indian and Pakistani officials has intensified regional volatility, underscoring the fragile state of India-Pakistan relations.

title: Chances of another war with India are real, warns Pakistan's defence minister
content: Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif warned on October 8, 2025, that 'chances of war with India are real,' stating that Pakistan would achieve a more favorable outcome in any future armed conflict. Speaking in an interview with Samaa TV, Asif cited ongoing threats from Indian political and military leaders, including statements by Indian Army Chief Gen Upendra Dwivedi, and emphasized that Pakistan remains vigilant. He claimed that Pakistan now has more international supporters and allies than it did six months prior, while asserting that India has lost backing from countries previously aligned with it. Asif also argued that India has never been a united nation except under Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, and that Pakistan was created in the name of Allah and demonstrated unity during the May 2025 confrontation despite internal challenges. He stated, 'At home, we argue and compete. In a fight with India, we come together.' His remarks follow Indian claims that Operation Sindoor—launched on May 7, 2025, in response to the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack—resulted in the destruction or damage of at least a dozen Pakistani military aircraft, including US-origin F-16 jets. India maintained that Pakistan sought to end hostilities on May 10 after sustained military strikes. Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh reiterated India’s stance that it can cross any border to protect its citizens and national integrity. The article was published by newsdrum.in on October 8, 2025.

title: Chances of war with India are real, warns Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif
content: Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif warned on October 7, 2025, in an interview with Samaa TV that 'chances of war with India are real,' citing ongoing tensions following statements by Indian political and military leaders. He stated that Pakistan would achieve 'a better result than before' in the event of armed conflict, emphasizing increased international support and national unity during the May 2025 clashes. Asif claimed Pakistan now has more allies than six months prior and that India had lost support from countries previously aligned with it. He also asserted that India has never been a united nation except under Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, while highlighting Pakistan’s unity in the face of external threats despite internal divisions. His remarks follow Indian military actions during Operation Sindoor, launched on May 7, 2025, in response to the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, which led to four days of intense clashes. India reported that at least a dozen Pakistani aircraft, including US-origin F-16s, were destroyed or damaged. The conflict ended on May 10 with an agreement to cease hostilities, which India claims was initiated by Pakistan. In response, Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh affirmed India’s right to cross any border to protect its citizens and national integrity. The article was published on October 8, 2025, by The Hindu.

title: Changing geostrategic undercurrents and Pakistan | The Express Tribune
content: Pakistan has experienced significant geostrategic shifts in 2024–2025, marked by three key developments. First, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif visited China in June 2024 to revitalize the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), now rebranded as CPEC 2.0, which emphasizes five pillars: exports, e-Pakistan, energy, environment, and equity/empowerment, organized into five strategic corridors: Growth, Innovation, Green, Livelihood-Enhancing, and Opening-Up/Regional Connectivity. Second, on September 17, 2025, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia formalized their strategic partnership through the 'Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA)', committing to mutual deterrence and treating aggression against one as aggression against the other. Third, on September 25, 2025, President Donald Trump met with Pakistani Army Chief Gen Asim Munir and PM Sharif at the White House, with US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in attendance. The closed-door 90-minute meeting focused on security, counterterrorism (CT), US support against Afghan threats, resumption of military programs, and the establishment of a 'Joint CT Command' in Pakistan. Trump signaled receptiveness to a conditional restart of the Coalition Support Fund (CSF), while Islamabad sought US investment, and Washington expressed interest in Pakistan’s critical minerals. These developments reflect a strategic reset in US-Pakistan relations, driven by deteriorating US-India ties due to India’s refusal to acknowledge US mediation in the May 2025 Indo-Pak conflict, trade delays, H1B visa issues, Russian oil purchases, and India’s strategic autonomy. The perceived Indian military failure in the May 2025 conflict, combined with the debate sparked by Ashley Tellis’s essay 'India's Great-Power Delusions' in Foreign Affairs (July-August 2025), has weakened US confidence in India’s strategic resolve. Pakistan’s diplomatic move of nominating Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize further exacerbated Indian alienation. Additionally, India’s exit from Iran after uncovering an Israeli proxy network and its alignment with Tel Aviv have undermined its regional ambitions, including access to Chahbahar Port and Afghan iron ore. The SMDA enhances Pakistan’s deterrence and regional relevance, displacing India from Saudi Arabia’s geostrategic framework. Iran, having reconciled with Saudi Arabia post-war with Israel, now sees the SMDA as a guarantor of regional security and is engaging in high-level talks with Saudi Arabia, signaling openness to a broader Islamic collective security model led by Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. The agreement’s expansion to other nations remains possible. Indian media has begun to acknowledge Pakistan’s rising diplomatic visibility and success. The article is authored by a retired major general with expertise in International Relations and Political Sociology.

title: Между Афганистаном и Пакистаном разгорается конфликт. Что нужно знать
content: Intense fighting erupted along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border on October 11, 2025, resulting in the deaths of 58 Pakistani military personnel and approximately 20 Afghan soldiers. The conflict stems from longstanding disputes over the Durand Line, a 2,400-km border established in 1893 during British India, which Afghanistan has never formally recognized due to its division of ethnic Pashtun tribes. Escalation was triggered by Afghanistan’s recent rapprochement with India, which plans to upgrade its technical representation in Kabul to a full embassy—seen by Islamabad as a strategic challenge to its influence in Afghanistan. Following attacks in Kabul and eastern Afghanistan on October 9, Afghan forces accused Pakistan of violating sovereignty, prompting Pakistan to retaliate with heavy artillery, armored vehicles, and drones. Pakistan targeted Nur Wali Mehsud, leader of the Pakistani Taliban, and denied involvement in the attacks. After diplomatic interventions by Iran, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, the Taliban withdrew from occupied border positions, calling the operation successful. Pakistan labeled the actions as provocation and reiterated accusations of Kabul harboring militants responsible for hundreds of military deaths since 2021. Militarily, Pakistan holds a significant advantage with a large, modern army and nuclear capabilities (60–170 warheads), while Afghanistan relies on less organized forces and terrain knowledge. Despite India’s strategic interest in countering Pakistan, it is unlikely to intervene directly, opting instead for diplomatic and economic pressure. Long-term risks include refugee flows, increased arms and drug trafficking, and regional instability. Regional powers such as Iran, China, and Gulf states may seek mediation to prevent escalation, as the conflict threatens trade routes and fuels extremism. The situation could strain Pakistan’s security across both Afghan and Indian fronts, while Afghanistan risks internal fragmentation and weakening of Taliban authority. Both nations may eventually seek third-party mediation or international involvement.

title: War of words
content: A renewed escalation in tensions between India and Pakistan followed a series of provocative statements by Indian officials in October 2025. Indian Army Chief Upendra Dwivedi warned that Pakistan could be 'erased from the world map' if it continues cross-border terrorism, claimed India would no longer show restraint as in 'Operation Sindoor', and urged troops to remain ready for action. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh accused Pakistan of expanding military infrastructure in the disputed Sir Creek region, stating that any aggression would trigger a response so strong it would 'change history and geography'. Air Force Chief Amar Preet Singh falsely claimed India shot down nine to ten Pakistani fighter jets, including two F-16s, during the May 2025 clash and asserted India's capability to strike deep inside Pakistan with precision. Pakistan responded sharply: Field Marshal Asim Munir, the army chief, vowed a 'swift retributory response', and the Inter-Services Public Relations labeled Indian statements as 'delusional, provocative and jingoistic', warning of 'cataclysmic devastation' and stating that 'the erasure would be mutual'. Analysts suggest India's rhetoric may serve domestic political aims—particularly to rally its Hindu nationalist base ahead of key state elections in Bihar and West Bengal—while also attempting to offset reputational damage from losing ground in the May conflict. However, the Indian military's aggressive posture may also reflect a desire to restore strategic credibility amid growing regional shifts. Pakistan's strengthened ties with the US, China's consistent support, and the Pakistan-Saudi defence pact have altered the geopolitical balance, making international backing for Indian military action unlikely. Indian media and former diplomats express concern over India's diplomatic isolation, the 'redrawing' of Pakistan's strategic playbook, and a potential 'alignment of adversarial powers' around India. Despite the risks, Pakistan maintains it must remain on high alert, especially as India's rhetoric hints at a changed 'rules of engagement' and possible future incursions. The writer, a former ambassador to the US, UK, and UN, emphasizes that Pakistan must prioritize its own security over external commitments, such as potential Middle East deployments under Trump's Gaza peace plan.

title: India Aggression and Pak Army - Daily Times
content: The article claims that India's political rhetoric under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh has intensified since early 2025, with statements such as 'we are fully prepared to teach Pakistan a lesson' and similar remarks at election rallies, which the author characterizes as irresponsible, a violation of international law, and a political tactic to distract from internal failures. The piece asserts that Pakistan has maintained a defensive, peace-seeking posture and responded to Indian aggression in May 2025 with a decisive military response, including the downing of Indian Rafale aircraft, which the author says was confirmed by satellite imagery and independent sources. The Pakistan Air Force is credited with a 'splendid' operation, and international media are cited as praising Pakistan’s military professionalism. The article highlights General Asim Munir’s leadership, emphasizing military reforms in AI, drones, cyber warfare, and air defense, and describes the Pakistani military as a 'regional deterrent force' recognized by global powers including the U.S., China, Turkey, and Gulf states. Diplomatically, Pakistan is said to have successfully presented evidence of Indian aggression at the UN and secured support from China, Turkey, Iran, and several European nations. The author argues that India is facing internal crises—religious discrimination, farmer protests, human rights violations in Kashmir, and rising poverty—and that war rhetoric is a diversionary strategy. Pakistan, according to the article, remains united, resilient, and prepared, with a strong military and a population that supports its defense institutions. The final message is clear: Pakistan seeks peace with dignity, not weakness, and will respond decisively to any aggression. The article concludes with the author’s identity as a freelance columnist and social activist.

title: Pakistan’s India-shaped chip on the shoulder, and why a peaceful coexistence is as elusive as ever
content: Pakistan's national identity, security policy, and political culture are deeply shaped by its perceived rivalry with India, described as an 'India-shaped chip' on its shoulder. Since Partition in 1947, India has been the central axis of Pakistan’s strategic and psychological orientation, with little focus on its borders with Iran or Afghanistan. Repeated conflicts—1947, 1965, 1971, and the 1999 Kargil War—entrenched the belief that India must be constantly checked. This narrative justifies high defense spending, military dominance in governance, and a political culture where softening toward India risks accusations of betrayal, imprisonment, or removal. The 2025 India–Pakistan conflict, triggered by India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty following a terrorist attack from Pakistan, led to a four-day exchange of missile, shelling, and drone attacks, ending in a ceasefire on May 10, 2025. Both sides now view each other with deep institutionalized mistrust: India suspects Pakistan of harboring militants, while Pakistan fears Indian aggression under the guise of counterterrorism or water security. Ceasefires are seen as tactical pauses, not progress. Nuclear posturing is central—Pakistan continues to modernize its arsenal, openly threatening 'full-spectrum retaliation' including first strikes, while India’s strategic alignment with the US, Japan, and Australia under the Quad reinforces its sense of superiority. Regional dynamics are further complicated by Pakistan’s deepening ties with China via the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, while India’s improving relations with China raise concerns about Beijing playing both sides. Diplomacy has collapsed since 2016, with nationalism in both countries rewarding confrontation. Civilian leaders in Pakistan risk being undermined by the military and public opinion if they pursue rapprochement. Meaningful peace would require fundamental shifts: formal risk-reduction mechanisms, transparent nuclear communication, rethinking Kashmir’s future, dismantling cross-border militant networks, easing restrictions in disputed territories, and joint investment in water-sharing and climate adaptation—none of which are politically feasible in 2025. The 'chip' is not just emotional; it is structural, embedded in state institutions and national myth. Even in sports, such as a recent cricket match where Pakistan’s captain threw the runners-up cheque on the ground and India refused to accept the trophy from Pakistani officials, tensions remain unresolved. Without a major external shock—such as an economic crisis, climate disaster, or transformative third-party intervention—the cycle of uneasy ceasefires, rhetorical wars, and real conflict will persist. For lasting peace, Pakistan must redefine India not as an existential threat but as an unavoidable neighbor—a psychological transformation that has so far eluded generations of leaders due to ideology, military dominance, and entrenched national myth.

title: The sudden risk of a broader South Asian war - Asia Times
content: On October 13, 2025, the Asia Times reported that an unprovoked cross-border attack by Afghan Taliban forces along Pakistan's western frontier—spanning areas from Angoor Adda to Chitral and Baramcha—has escalated regional tensions. Pakistan reported 23 soldiers killed and at least 29 injured, with an Afghan spokesman claiming 58 fatalities. Pakistan's military claimed to have killed over 200 Taliban fighters in retaliation. The attack coincided with Afghanistan's acting foreign minister visiting India, fueling suspicions of a strategic shift in Kabul’s foreign policy. The incident marks a turning point in South Asia’s security landscape, as the Taliban’s aggression challenges Pakistan’s long-standing support for an Afghan-led peace process and signals a move toward asserting autonomy through force. Pakistan faces a potential two-front threat: from Afghanistan and possibly from India, which has deepened quiet ties with the Taliban. China, whose Belt and Road Initiative depends on stability via the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), is expected to push for de-escalation while supporting Pakistan economically and intelligence-wise. Saudi Arabia, having recently signed a defense cooperation pact with Pakistan, is likely to provide financial and logistical backing to counterbalance Iranian influence. India, while seeking to prevent Afghanistan from becoming a haven for anti-India groups, may exploit the crisis to pressure Pakistan, particularly in Kashmir. A coordinated response between China, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia could emerge, creating a strategic alignment that constrains Indian ambitions. The outcome hinges on Pakistan’s ability to respond firmly yet non-escalatorily, leveraging diplomatic ties to isolate Kabul. The attack is described not as an isolated incident but as a stress test for regional alliances, with the potential to trigger a broader South Asian conflict if mismanaged.

title: 'New normal of response': Military warns any future Pak-India hostilities might lead to 'cataclysmic devastation'
content: Pakistan's military, through its Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), warned on October 4, 2025, that any future hostilities with India could result in 'cataclysmic devastation' and pledged a 'resolute response, without any qualms or restraint.' The statement followed provocative remarks by Indian civil-military leadership, including Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, who claimed India has the capability to defeat all challenges, and Army Chief General Upendra Dwivedi, who warned Pakistan against state-sponsored terrorism. Indian Air Force Chief Amar Preet Singh falsely claimed to have downed five Pakistani F-16 and JF-17 fighter jets during the May 2025 conflict. The ISPR rejected India's narrative, accusing it of 'delusional, provocative and jingoistic' rhetoric and asserting that India is the 'epicentre of regional instability' and the true source of cross-border terrorism. Pakistan emphasized it has established a 'new normal of response'—swift, decisive, and destructive—and will shatter the myth of geographic immunity by striking deep into Indian territory. The announcement came shortly after Pakistan created the Army Rocket Force Command in August 2025, a new long-range conventional strike capability designed to operate ballistic, cruise, and potentially hypersonic missiles without resorting to nuclear weapons. This development followed the May 2025 four-day conflict, which began after an attack on Hindu tourists in occupied Kashmir, which India blamed on Pakistan without evidence. Pakistan denied involvement, calling India’s account 'replete with fabrications.' During the conflict, both sides used fighter jets, missiles, artillery, and drones, killing dozens; Pakistan claimed to have downed six Indian jets, including Rafales, while India acknowledged 'some losses' but denied the full extent. The ISPR warned that India’s 'collective amnesia' and renewed aggression could lead to 'serious consequences for peace and stability' in South Asia.
